turns.doctor_question: Hi, it’s nice to meet you. What brings you in today?
turns.patient_response:
Well, it's nice to meet you too, Doctor. I suppose what really made me finally make the appointment and come all the way down here today is... well, it's my eating. It's just gotten all turned around lately. And I mean completely topsy-turvy. 

You see, I'm at home most of the day now, and you'd think I'd have a proper schedule, maybe make myself a nice little sandwich or heat up some soup at noon like I always used to, but lately... some days I just completely forget lunch. The whole afternoon will go by, the sun will start going down, and I'll look at the clock and realize I haven't had a single bite to eat since the morning. 

But then, on the other hand, there are these other days where I just stand right there at the kitchen counter—not even bothering to sit down at the table, just standing there by the sink—and I'll just eat crackers, or whatever sweets I have sitting in the pantry. Just mindlessly eating them one after another. And the strangest part of it all is that nothing even tastes right anymore. I'll be chewing on a cookie or a saltine and it's like dust in my mouth, absolutely no flavor at all, but I just keep standing there eating it anyway. It's just so unusual for me, and I just couldn't figure out why my appetite is so all over the place...

symptom_reasoning.S026: The patient explicitly describes significant fluctuations in their appetite, noting they sometimes forget to eat entirely and other times mindlessly eat snacks, stating their 'appetite is so all over the place.'

turns.doctor_question: Have you actually lost your sense of taste?
turns.patient_response:
Well, I... I wouldn't say I've completely lost it, no. It's not like when you get a terrible head cold and you literally can't taste a single thing, not even a strong peppermint. It's not like that. So the mechanics of it, I suppose, the actual taste buds, they must still be working on some level. 

But it's just... the enjoyment of it, the richness of the flavor, that's what's gone. It's like the volume has been turned way, way down on everything. So no, I haven't gone completely numb in the mouth or anything like that. It's more of a... a dullness. A terrible, persistent dullness that just won't go away, no matter what I try to eat. I even tried putting extra pepper on my eggs the other morning, thinking maybe I just needed to spice things up, but it just tasted like hot dust. turns.doctor_question: Have you also been enjoying other things less than usual?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, yes. Yes, I have. It's funny you ask that, because my daughter was just saying the exact same thing to me on the phone the other day. You see, I have always been a very active person, very involved with my friends and my little community here. I used to look forward to my watercolor class on Tuesday mornings—we've been painting landscapes lately, and I just loved mixing the greens and blues to get the trees just right. And then there's the quilting circle on Thursdays, which I've been a part of for, oh, it must be fifteen years now. We're working on a beautiful star pattern for the church bazaar. And my Sunday book club, too! I used to just love all of it, every single bit of it. 

I'd get my little canvas tote bag ready the night before, make sure I had my brushes or my thimbles or whatever book we were reading—we were supposed to read a lovely historical novel this month, though I haven't even opened it. Because lately... well, I'll pack my bag the night before, just like always, mostly out of habit, I suppose. I'll set it right there by the front door so I don't forget it. And then the morning comes, and it's time to put my coat on and walk down to the community center, and I just... I look at the bag, and I look at the door, and I just can't make myself care enough to go. 

I often just leave the bag sitting right there by the door. It's the strangest thing, just this complete lack of interest in the things that used to be the absolute highlights of my week. I'll just sit back down in my armchair instead and watch the cars go by out the living room window, and I'll think about how I should be at quilting, how the ladies are probably wondering where I am, but I just don't have the heart for it anymore. It's just like the food, really. It feels like all the color and the joy have just been washed right out of my routine, and I just can't seem to muster up the energy to care about any of my hobbies at all...

turns.doctor_question: Have you been feeling down or depressed most days?
turns.patient_response:
Well, yes. Yes, I really have. It's... it's hard to explain without sounding silly, but most mornings I wake up with this terrible, heavy, low feeling. It settles right over me the moment I open my eyes. I've always been an early riser, you know, up at six-thirty every morning to get the coffee going and pull the curtains open, but lately... well, I just lie there. It's like the color has completely gone out of the day before I even manage to get dressed. 

I'll look over at my closet, at the nice blouses I have hung up in there, and I just feel so weighed down by it all. The sun could be shining right through the window, but everything just feels gray and dreary to me. And it just stays with me, that heavy feeling, following me from the bedroom to the kitchen, right to that armchair I mentioned. Day in and day out, it's just this constant, low cloud hovering right over my head. I just can't seem to shake it, no matter how hard I try to put on a brave face for the neighbors or when my daughter calls. So, yes, I'd say I feel very down almost every single day now, from the very minute I wake up.

turns.doctor_question: Have you had thoughts that life isn’t worth living, or thoughts of harming yourself?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, well... that's a difficult question, isn't it? It's not the sort of thing you want to admit to, especially when you've always prided yourself on being strong for your family. I don't want to worry my daughter, you know. She has her own life, her own family, her job at the bank—she's a loan officer, very busy, always running here and there. I wouldn't want to add to her plate. 

But... well, to be completely honest with you, doctor, I have had some dark thoughts lately. I want to be very clear, though—I haven't made any sort of plan. I wouldn't do that. I don't have pills hidden away or anything terrible like that. I wouldn't take my own life, I really wouldn't. It's against my beliefs, and it would just leave such a mess for everyone else to clean up. I've always been very tidy, very organized, and I couldn't bear the thought of leaving my daughter to sort through that kind of tragedy.

It's just that... well, with this heavy feeling every day, sitting in that armchair and looking at the canvas tote bag by the door, knowing I'm not going to quilting or book club... I just catch myself thinking sometimes. I think about how tired I am, how gray everything is, and I think... well, if I just went to sleep one night and simply didn't wake up the next morning... it might not be the worst thing. It might actually be a bit of a relief. A relief for me, to be free of this awful dullness, and a relief for my family, so they wouldn't have to worry about their poor old mother sitting alone in her house all day. It's just a passing thought, usually when I'm lying in bed before the sun comes up, but it's there. Just this quiet little wish that maybe I could just slip away peacefully and not have to face another heavy day.

turns.doctor_question: Did something stressful happen in your life around the time all of this started?
turns.patient_response:
Well, yes, actually. It's funny you should ask about the timing, because I've thought about that quite a bit while sitting in my armchair. It hasn't always been like this, you know. I used to have so much energy, like I said about my watercolor class and the quilting circle. But this whole change, this awful heaviness and losing interest in everything... it's been going on for about a year and five months now. 

I know the exact timeline because it started right around the time my sister's health took a very serious turn. My sister, Martha—she's two years older than me, lives over in the next county, in a lovely little ranch house she and her husband bought back in the seventies. We've always been so close, talking on the phone every Sunday evening without fail. But then, about a year and a half ago—well, a year and five months, to be precise—she had this terrible fall in her kitchen. She was just reaching for a can of soup on the top shelf, lost her balance, and down she went. Broke her hip, and at our age, well, you know how devastating that can be. 

It was just so stressful. I was driving back and forth to the hospital, then to the rehabilitation center, trying to make sure she was getting the right care, dealing with her doctors, trying to help her husband, who was just beside himself with worry. He's a sweet man, but he doesn't handle medical things well at all. I was trying to be strong for everyone, packing overnight bags, making casseroles so they'd have something to eat... and it just took so much out of me. It was terrifying seeing her so frail, and I think the worry just seeped right into my bones. That's when I first started noticing that I didn't want to go to my book club, and then the heavy feeling in the mornings started creeping in, and it just hasn't lifted since. So yes, it's been about a year and five months since all of this started, right when Martha had her accident.

turns.doctor_question: Before this began a year and five months ago, have you ever had another period in your life when you felt depressed like this for weeks at a time?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, goodness, no. No, I really haven't. I was actually just thinking about that the other day when I was sitting in my chair, looking over at the bookshelf where I keep all the old family photo albums. My daughter had brought them down from the attic for me last Christmas... or was it Thanksgiving? No, it must have been Christmas, because I remember we had the red poinsettia tablecloth out on the dining table. Anyway, I was thinking about all those years, looking at pictures from my twenties and thirties, and I realized I've always been such a busy, cheerful person. 

Even when my late husband passed away—God rest his soul, that was back in ninety-eight, a sudden heart attack, just terrible—I was heartbroken, of course. Completely devastated. We had a beautiful service for him at the First Methodist church, flowers everywhere. But even with all that grief, it was a... well, a normal kind of sadness, if that makes sense. I still got out of bed every morning. I still made sure the house was spotless, I still went down to the Piggly Wiggly for my groceries, and I kept up with my garden. I never had this... this awful, paralyzing heaviness that I have now. 

I've always been a doer, doctor. When the girls were little, I was PTA president for three years running, organizing bake sales and holiday pageants, always running the carpool. I always had a smile on my face and a casserole in the oven. Even when things were tough, like when the local plant closed down in the eighties and money was terribly tight for a while, I just rolled up my sleeves and found ways to make do. I've never, ever had a time in my life where I just sat around for weeks on end, feeling gray and empty like this. This whole terrible cloud is completely new to me. It's just so unlike me, which is why my daughter finally insisted I come talk to someone. So, no, before Martha's fall a year and five months ago, I had never experienced anything even remotely like this. I was always right as rain.
